sentences.text: He came back the next day.
And the day after that.
He did not do anything clever.
That is the part he told his own children, years later, when they asked, and they were always disappointed by it.
He did not sing to her.
He did not bring her anything, because what do you bring.
He did not try to wake her, because it seemed to him that waking somebody who is carrying something heavy is a good way to make them drop it on their foot.
He sat on the cold stone at four metres, and he stayed for an hour, and then he went home.
Sometimes he read out loud, because the silence up there had a quality that made him want to put something into it.
He read a book about a shipwreck, which he had read twice already, and he skipped the boring middle both times.

Once he told her, at length and with considerable feeling, about a disagreement he had had with his brother — a disagreement which had seemed enormous at eight in the morning and which had somehow got smaller and smaller as he described it, until by the end of the telling it had shrunk to roughly the size of a misunderstanding about a bicycle pump, which is what it had actually been all along.
He talked to her for fourteen days.
On the eleventh day the snow around the hollow had gone soft at the edges.
He noticed it on the way up: the clean line had lost its cleanness.
It had begun to fray.
On the twelfth day there was water running under the snow.

He could hear it before he could see it — a thin sound, very cold, like a wire being drawn — and when he knelt down and pushed the crust with his thumb it came away and there were threads of water underneath, going down the mountain in a hurry, as though they had been waiting a long time and had somewhere to be.
The bear did not wake while he was there.
Not once, in twelve days.
He went up on the thirteenth day and the hollow was empty.
It was warm.

That was the thing that stopped him at the edge of it — the hollow was warm, and it smelled of wet stone and crushed grass and, faintly, of animal, and there was a shallow dish pressed into the ground where something very large had lain for a very long time.
There were no tracks leading away.
He looked.
He looked for most of an hour, in widening circles, and the ground was soft enough that there should have been tracks, and there were none.
He went down the mountain with his coat over his arm because he did not need it.
In the valley the almond tree by the church had opened.
All of it.
Every bud on every branch, all at once, in a single afternoon, as though the tree had been standing there for nine weeks with its arms folded waiting for somebody to give it permission.

The petals were coming off it already in the warm air and going along the road in drifts, and two of the Sokol children were running through them, and the smell of it reached him before he got to the gate.
His mother was in the doorway with a basket on her hip.
"There you are," she said.
"Spring, at last.
About time." "Did you see the tree?" "I saw it.
Sixty years I've been looking at that tree." She shifted the basket.
"The weather owes nobody an explanation." Tolek considered telling her.
He thought about it the whole way across the yard, and he decided — for reasons he could not have given you at the time and could give you perfectly well now — that it was not his to tell.
"No," he agreed.
"It doesn't." And he went to wash his hands.
